articles.title: Why Are India and the US Still Struggling to Close a Trade Deal? - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Why Are India and the US Still Struggling to Close a Trade Deal?  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
India and the United States have once again failed to break through a prolonged impasse in negotiations over a bilateral trade agreement, underscoring the growing difficulty of managing economic ties between two countries that have otherwise sought to deepen their strategic partnership.
Senior officials on both sides have signalled that negotiations have effectively reached a standstill. India’s Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman recently described the talks as having reached a “plateau”, while US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said a deal was not imminent.
The latest setback comes despite an agreement reached in February that had appeared to provide a path towards a broader trade deal. That framework reduced the punitive US tariff on most Indian goods from 50% to 18%, after an earlier round of negotiations collapsed.
The situation has since become more complicated. The US Supreme Court’s decision to invalidate President Donald Trump’s use of emergency powers to impose sweeping global tariffs resulted in a 10% baseline tariff, but it did not resolve the wider disagreements between Washington and New Delhi.
Why Have the Talks Stalled?
The central problem is that the two countries continue to have different priorities over market access, tariffs and India’s energy relationship with Russia.
One of the most immediate complications is a new US law that could allow tariffs of up to 100% on Indian goods because of India’s continued purchases of Russian oil. New Delhi has not significantly reduced those purchases, despite pressure from Washington.
For India, accepting potentially much higher tariffs would undermine its efforts to obtain treatment comparable to that given to other major Asian trading partners, including Vietnam and China. For Washington, however, India’s energy purchases have become part of a broader effort to pressure countries that continue to buy Russian commodities and, in the US view, indirectly support Moscow’s war effort in Ukraine.
The disagreement therefore extends beyond conventional trade negotiations. Tariff policy has increasingly become connected to US foreign policy objectives, while India continues to defend its freedom to determine its own energy supplies.
Another source of uncertainty is a US Section 301 investigation into several countries over alleged excess industrial capacity. Washington is examining whether overproduction in those economies is harming or undercutting American industries.
Until the investigation is completed, India cannot be certain what additional tariffs its exporters could eventually face. That uncertainty makes it harder for New Delhi to determine how far it should go in offering concessions as part of a trade agreement.
The broader relationship has also faced tensions over the past year. A US military attack on a ship off Oman that killed three Indian seafarers caused friction, while India rejected Trump’s repeated claims that he had played a role in brokering a ceasefire between India and Pakistan.
These disputes have added to an already complicated political environment surrounding the trade negotiations.
What Is at Stake for India?
The economic consequences are significant because the United States is India’s largest export market.
Indian goods exports to the US increased to $42.79 billion between April and August, compared with $40.39 billion during the same period a year earlier. During the 2025/26 financial year, India recorded a trade surplus of almost $34 billion with the United States.
So far, Indian exports have shown considerable resilience despite the tariff uncertainty. New Delhi has also pointed out that some of its major export categories, including generic pharmaceuticals and smartphones, are not currently covered by the 10% baseline tariff.
But the situation could become considerably more difficult if additional US tariffs are imposed.
Higher tariffs could increase costs for Indian exporters, weaken business confidence and put further pressure on the Indian rupee, which is already trading close to record lows. Companies that depend heavily on access to the US market would face particularly strong pressure to either absorb the additional costs or pass them on to American consumers.
For India, therefore, the objective is not simply to secure a trade agreement. It is to obtain predictable access to one of its most important export markets without sacrificing politically sensitive sectors or its energy policy.
What Does India Want?
New Delhi’s negotiating position reflects the political importance of agriculture.
India has sought to protect sectors such as dairy, poultry, rice and wheat from extensive market-opening commitments. These sectors are particularly sensitive because millions of farmers depend on them and because agricultural liberalisation has significant domestic political consequences.
At the same time, India wants better tariff treatment for its exporters and greater certainty over the tariffs they will face in the US market.
That creates a difficult balancing act. New Delhi wants increased access to the American market, but it does not want to offer concessions in politically sensitive sectors without knowing whether those concessions will produce sufficiently stable and favourable treatment for Indian exports.
What Does Washington Want?
The Trump administration has placed greater emphasis on reducing India’s purchases of Russian crude.
Washington argues that India’s continued purchases of Russian oil provide Moscow with an important source of revenue and therefore indirectly support its ability to sustain the war in Ukraine.
India rejects the idea that its energy purchases should be dictated by geopolitical pressure. It argues that decisions over energy sourcing are primarily driven by the needs of its population of more than 1.4 billion people.
Russian crude became particularly important for India after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine because it was available at substantial discounts. The continuing conflict in the Middle East has made energy security even more important by increasing uncertainty over global supplies and shipping routes.
This makes India’s position difficult to change quickly. Reducing Russian oil imports could satisfy an important US demand, but it could also raise India’s energy costs and expose the country to greater volatility in global energy markets.
Can the Talks Still Be Revived?
The negotiations are not necessarily heading for a permanent breakdown.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected to visit India later this month, potentially creating an opportunity for the two sides to reassess their positions. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Trump also spoke by phone on September 30 and are expected to speak again to review progress.
Modi is expected to travel to the United States in December for a G20 leaders’ meeting, providing another potential opportunity for political intervention if negotiations remain stalled.
The challenge is that the two sides now need to resolve issues that extend beyond tariffs.
India wants greater certainty and improved access to the US market while protecting agriculture and maintaining flexibility over energy imports. Washington wants deeper market access for American goods and stronger alignment from New Delhi on Russian oil.
That combination has made the trade negotiations as much a test of the broader India-US relationship as a conventional economic agreement.
A compromise remains possible, particularly if political leaders decide that the strategic importance of the relationship outweighs the remaining economic disagreements. But until Washington clarifies the future tariff regime and New Delhi determines how far it is willing to move on Russian oil and agricultural market access, a comprehensive trade deal is likely to remain difficult to reach.

articles.title: RBI raises India’s GDP forecast to 7.1%, says 'economy strong' - CNBC TV18

articles.full_text:
3 Min Read
The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has raised its forecast for India's gross domestic product (GDP) growth for the financial year 2027 to 7.1%.
The RBI MPC had earlier forecast 6.7% growth for FY27 in August.
The upgrade comes after the National Statistical Office (NSO) estimated real GDP growth at 7.8% in Q1 FY27, which the RBI said was higher than expected.
The central bank also projected growth at 7.20% for Q2 of the current financial year, 6.90% for Q3 and 6.80% for Q4.
Current GDP Forecast Earlier GDP Forecast FY27 7.10% 6.70% Q2 FY27 7.20% 6.40% Q3 FY27 6.90% 6.50% Q4 FY27 6.80% 6.80% Q1 FY28 7.10% 7.30% 
Growth for Q1 FY28 is also projected at 7.1%.
Ahead of the announcement, CNBC-TV18 poll of economists reflected a largely divided view. Half of the respondents expected the RBI to raise its FY27 GDP growth forecast to 6.8%-7%, while the remaining half expected a sharper upward revision to 7%-7.2%.
"Domestic economic activity exhibited resilience. Growth was driven by resilient private consumption and strong investment activity," RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said.
Strong capacity utilisation, robust credit flows and the government's infrastructure push are expected to sustain investment activity, while continued momentum in services and stable employment conditions are likely to support urban demand.
However, the central bank flagged risks from elevated energy prices and supply-chain pressures due to lingering impacts of the West Asia war. A deficient southwest monsoon and strong El Nino conditions also pose risks to agriculture and rural demand.
The committee also unanimously decided to hike repo rate by 25 bps to 5.50%
RBI shifts stance to calibrated tightening
In addition to the rate hike, the central bank changed its stance to "calibrated tightening".
"Given current conditions, rate cuts are off the table in the near term. Policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause, depending on evolving conditions," the governor said.
However, the change in stance was not unanimous. Two MPC members — Nagesh Kumar and Ram Singh — favoured retaining the neutral stance.
Hawkish on inflation
The RBI also raised its FY27 CPI inflation forecast to 5.2%, from its previous projection of 5.0%.
CPI inflation rose to 4.8% in August from 4.5% in July, while core inflation increased to 4.2%. The RBI said inflation pressures had become more broad-based, with food and fuel prices contributing to the rise.
It expects CPI inflation at 4.9% in Q2, 6% in Q3 and 5.7% in Q4, with inflation projected at 5.6% in Q1 FY28. Core inflation is projected at 4.4% for FY27.

Kazakhstan has announced the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding with Uzbekistan and the UAE for a rail connection to Pakistan. The three countries want to connect Central Asia to the Indian Ocean, but infrastructure is currently lacking. For now, they agreed to evaluate their options before starting implementation.
The Central Asia–South Asia (CASA) railway would start in Kazakhstan, transit Uzbekistan and Afghanistan and link up to Pakistani ports. There has been international interest in such a rail connection for over two years now, but nothing tangible has happened yet to implement it. The region is geographically and politically complex, which makes implementation difficult.

“Bringing these capabilities together will enable us to move on to the practical development of the CASA project and the identification of the best mechanisms for its implementation”, the ministry added.

articles.title: 25 Years, One Development Journey: How Gujarat Became the Launchpad for Modi’s National Vision - Indianmasterminds
articles.summary: 25 Years, One Development Journey: How Gujarat Became the Launchpad for Modi’s National Vision  Indianmasterminds
articles.full_text:
Gandhinagar: Twenty-five years ago, on October 7, 2001, Narendra Modi became the Chief Minister of Gujarat. The state was then recovering from the devastating earthquake and faced the immediate challenge of rebuilding infrastructure as well as public confidence.
What followed was a development and governance journey that placed roads, electricity, water, education, agriculture and industry at the centre of Gujarat’s transformation. Twenty-five years later, that journey has expanded to the national level, with the vision of building a Viksit Bharat by 2047.
From Rebuilding Gujarat to a People-Centric Development Model
During his 13-year tenure as Gujarat Chief Minister from 2001 to 2014, Modi’s administration focused on reviewing policies and administrative systems while expanding development across key sectors.
Several initiatives attempted to bring government programmes closer to citizens. Shala Praveshotsav and Gunotsav focused on education, while Krushi Mahotsav and Pashu Arogya Mela brought attention to agriculture and animal healthcare. Khel Mahakumbh expanded public participation in sports, while Vibrant Gujarat developed into a platform to position the state as an investment and industrial destination.
Technology also became an important part of governance. The SWAGAT grievance-redressal initiative allowed citizens to place their concerns before the government and seek responses. The initiative later became part of the wider governance experience associated with Modi’s Gujarat tenure.
The governance approach was also linked to the Panchamrit vision of Jan Shakti, Jal Shakti, Gyan Shakti, Urja Shakti and Raksha Shakti, placing people, resources, knowledge, energy and security within a broader development framework.

Gujarat Experience Moves to the National Stage
When Modi became Prime Minister in 2014, the Gujarat experience became part of a larger national development agenda. The approach of combining government programmes with public participation was reflected in several major national initiatives.
Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana, Swachh Bharat, Nal Se Jal and Khelo India brought healthcare, sanitation, drinking water and sports into the national development framework.
The Union Cabinet’s October 6, 2026 resolution marking Modi’s 25 years as head of government also highlighted the link between Gujarat and national governance. It specifically noted how the experience of SWAGAT informed the later PRAGATI platform, while Gujarat’s Jyotigram experience influenced approaches to electricity access.
This Gujarat-to-India transition has also extended into technology, infrastructure, manufacturing and self-reliance.
Aatmanirbhar Bharat and India’s Expanding Capabilities
Modi completed 12 years as Prime Minister in 2026, taking his combined tenure as Gujarat Chief Minister and Prime Minister to 25 years.
Since 2014, the national development agenda has expanded across the economy, infrastructure, defence, trade, aviation, railways, ports and digital infrastructure. Aatmanirbhar Bharat has emerged as a major theme, with greater emphasis on domestic manufacturing, technology and strategic capabilities.
The government’s October 2026 resolution highlighted the growth of public capital expenditure, highways, railway electrification, electronics production, defence manufacturing and semiconductors as part of this broader self-reliance push.
India’s growing international role has also been reflected in initiatives such as Vaccine Maitri, the International Solar Alliance and Operation Sindoor, alongside a wider effort to strengthen India’s position in global development and strategic affairs.
Gujarat Continues to Receive Major Development Projects
The 25-year journey has also been accompanied by major infrastructure, manufacturing, technology, financial and energy projects in Gujarat.
Among the key projects and developments highlighted during this period are:
- ₹20,667-crore Ahmedabad-Dholera rail project approved to improve connectivity to Dholera, Dholera Airport and Lothal.
- ₹5,800-crore Ahmedabad-Dholera Expressway, covering 109 km, approved.
- 20-year tax holiday for institutions in GIFT City announced in Union Budget 2026-27.
- Development projects worth over ₹35,200 crore dedicated to Gujarat in September 2026.
- Suzuki e-VITARA launched from Hansalpur, with local hybrid battery electrode production. Made-in-India EVs are exported to over 100 countries.
- Three projects worth ₹3,645 crore inaugurated at the Khavda Renewable Energy Park.
- Ahmedabad will host the 2030 Commonwealth Games.
- Six semiconductor projects approved in Gujarat under the India Semiconductor Mission.
- Gujarat Forensic Sciences University became National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU) and an Institution of National Importance in 2020.
- 1,144 houses built in Rajkot under the Light House Project using modern technology.
- IFSCA became operational in GIFT City.
- India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX) established in GIFT City.
- Foundation stone laid for a Bulk Drug Park in Bharuch to boost pharmaceutical manufacturing.
- PM MITRA Park approved at Navsari among seven mega textile parks under the national scheme.
- Foundation stone laid for the world’s first CNG terminal at Bhavnagar Port.
- Narendra Modi Stadium constructed in Ahmedabad as a major international cricket venue.
₹20,000-crore Dahod railway facility developed to manufacture 9,000-horsepower electric freight locomotives under Make in India.
In May 2025, the Dahod facility was dedicated to the nation, with plans to produce 1,200 9,000-HP electric locomotives.
The Next Destination: Viksit Bharat @2047
The significance of the 25-year journey lies not only in the number of projects but also in the transition from a state-focused development model to a national vision.
Gujarat remains an important part of that journey, with investments and projects spanning semiconductors, renewable energy, electric vehicles, railways, pharmaceuticals, textiles, financial services and industrial infrastructure.
The next stated milestone is Viksit Bharat @2047. The vision seeks to build on India’s economic strength, technological capabilities, infrastructure and global role while advancing the goal of a more self-reliant country.
From Gujarat’s post-earthquake reconstruction in 2001 to India’s development and self-reliance agenda in 2026, Narendra Modi’s 25-year public service journey has moved through different phases of governance. Its continuing focus remains development, public participation, technology, infrastructure and nation-building, with Gujarat continuing to play a significant role in the larger national development story.

Indian police detained opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and several lawmakers for the third time in two days on Wednesday as they launched an unannounced protest demanding the resignation of the election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Opposition parties, their student units, and the “cockroach” youth movement have been staging almost daily demonstrations seeking Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, after the Indian Express newspaper last month reported disagreements within the poll panel over updating voter lists, stoking concerns over its neutrality.
Opposition lawmakers led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi protested on Tuesday as well, seeking a meeting with Kumar and his deputies, before police broke up their gathering and briefly detained them.
Wednesday’s protest began after a lunch meeting of lawmakers that Congress organised at a restaurant in central Delhi, close to the Jantar Mantar site where authorities permit demonstrations.
“Yesterday … Delhi Police stopped us and said you cannot protest here … so today … we will go to the designated protest site, sit there, and tell the country that, for us, Gyanesh Kumar is not the legitimate commissioner,” Gandhi told reporters, referring to Jantar Mantar.
“The people who have done this (vote theft) are traitors … Gyanesh Kumar will have to resign,” he said, before boarding a bus that was to take the lawmakers to Jantar Mantar.
New political challenge to Modi
Lawmakers in the bus held posters against the windows that said, “no vote theft, no democracy theft”, and “election commission, not BJP commission”, referring to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party.
Hundreds of Congress members accompanied the bus on foot amid heavy deployment of police and paramilitary personnel in riot gear. Police also closed the road leading to Jantar Mantar, forcing the bus to take a detour.
Gandhi later stepped out of the bus, with a live feed on his party’s YouTube channel showing him standing at the centre of a crowd of protesters and security personnel, while his sister Priyanka Vadra and other lawmakers sprawled out on the road.
Visuals showed security personnel hauling Gandhi and Vadra into separate vehicles and taking them away.
There was no immediate comment from the police on the detentions.
The demonstrations present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) youth movement forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.
Kumar has not commented on the voter lists issue but the election commission and BJP have denied accusations of wrongdoing.

articles.title: Delayed Adulthood for Gen Z: Why Young Indians Wait - Dainik Jagran MP CG
articles.summary: Delayed Adulthood for Gen Z: Why Young Indians Wait  Dainik Jagran MP CG
articles.full_text:
Digital Desk
Rising living costs, job insecurity and housing pressures are pushing many young Indians to delay independence, marriage and starting families.
For many young Indians, moving out, getting married and starting a family are not being rejected — they are being postponed. Rising costs, uncertain employment and housing pressures are making financial stability feel like a prerequisite for adulthood.
For generations, adulthood in India followed a familiar sequence: finish education, find a job, become financially independent, get married and eventually start a family.
That sequence is becoming less predictable.
For many young Indians, particularly in urban areas, the problem is not a rejection of marriage, family or independence. It is the growing difficulty of achieving the financial stability that makes those decisions feel possible.
A recent UNFPA Demographic Futures Survey offers an important correction to the popular narrative about young people. More than two-thirds of young respondents globally said they wanted to marry or live with a partner, while financial security, stable employment and emotional readiness emerged as major conditions for parenthood. The survey included more than 108,000 internet-connected people aged 18–39 across 73 countries; its India findings similarly point to economic and housing constraints shaping family decisions.
The story, therefore, is not simply that Gen Z does not want adulthood.
It is that adulthood is becoming more expensive.
Independence now has a price tag
Leaving home once represented a major milestone.
Today, in many cities, it can mean paying a substantial share of a starting salary toward rent, transport, food, utilities and other basic expenses before saving anything meaningful.
Recent reporting has highlighted young professionals returning to their family homes because high rents, limited savings and employment uncertainty make independent living financially difficult.
Living with parents is not automatically evidence of economic failure. In India, multigenerational households have always been common.
What is changing is the reason some young adults remain at home.
For some, it is a choice based on family preference. For others, it is simply the financially rational option.
When staying at home allows a young worker to save instead of spending a large portion of income on rent, independence becomes less about moving out and more about building financial security.
That changes the meaning of adulthood itself.
Marriage is increasingly becoming a financial decision
Marriage has never been purely an economic institution, but money has always mattered.
Today, the financial calculation can begin long before the wedding.
Young people may consider housing, job stability, wedding expenses, childcare, education costs and whether two incomes will be sufficient to maintain the lifestyle they expect.
UNFPA's 2025 State of World Population report found that financial limitations were among the biggest barriers to people achieving their desired family size in India, while job insecurity and housing constraints were also significant factors.
The newer 2026 Demographic Futures Survey reinforces the same broader point: young people are not necessarily abandoning family aspirations. They are asking whether the economic conditions exist to build the family life they want.
That distinction matters.
If young people delay marriage because they want a stable income first, the response should not be moral panic about changing values.
It should be a serious conversation about why stable adulthood has become harder to afford.
The first job has become more important than ever
A delayed career can produce a chain reaction.
A graduate may spend additional years preparing for competitive examinations, searching for suitable employment, changing jobs or building skills. During that period, savings may remain limited and financial dependence on parents may continue.
India's labour-market data show that employment conditions remain uneven. The latest monthly PLFS data available from the Ministry of Statistics showed an overall unemployment rate of 5.1% for people aged 15 and above in July 2026, with urban unemployment at 6.7%.
The unemployment rate alone, however, does not capture the entire transition into adulthood.
A young person can technically be employed and still struggle to afford independent housing, build savings or plan for a family.
That is why the quality and stability of the first few years of employment matter.
A job that pays the bills today but offers little security tomorrow can still postpone major life decisions.
Housing is becoming part of the family debate
The cost of housing has implications far beyond the real-estate sector.
If young workers cannot afford a reasonably located home, they may delay moving out.
If couples cannot afford adequate housing, they may delay marriage.
If housing is available but childcare and education costs are perceived as unaffordable, they may postpone having children.
This creates a broader affordability problem in which housing, employment and family formation become interconnected.
The UNFPA's research specifically identifies housing and economic constraints as important obstacles to partnership and parenthood.
For policymakers, that means youth policy cannot stop at employment statistics.
Affordable rental housing, urban transport, childcare, healthcare and stable employment all influence whether young adults can build independent lives.
The burden is not equally shared
Delayed adulthood also has a gender dimension.
Young women may face a difficult combination of career expectations, family expectations and unequal domestic responsibilities.
The 2026 UNFPA India findings note that young women spend substantially more time on unpaid housework and caregiving than young men, while paid-work participation is also much lower among young women.
That matters for family formation.
If having children is perceived as requiring women to sacrifice career progression disproportionately, the decision to start a family can become much more complicated.
The solution cannot simply be to tell women to “balance” everything.
Families, employers and public policy have to make caregiving more compatible with employment.
Paid parental leave, flexible work, affordable childcare and a more equal distribution of household responsibilities are not merely social-policy ideas.
They can directly affect whether young people feel capable of forming families.
Parents are becoming the financial bridge
One of the least discussed consequences of delayed adulthood is the changing role of parents.
A young adult who cannot afford independent living may remain at home longer.
A graduate preparing for examinations may depend on family savings.
A newly employed person may still need parental support for housing or major expenses.
In families that can provide this support, the transition may be manageable.
In lower- and middle-income households, however, prolonged dependence can put pressure on savings and postpone other family goals.
This connects delayed adulthood to the broader issue of household financial stress.
The burden of an uncertain labour market does not necessarily disappear when a young person turns 25 or 30.
It can simply move from the individual's bank account to the household balance sheet.
Young Indians are not necessarily less ambitious
There is another mistake in the delayed-adulthood debate: assuming that postponement means a lack of ambition.
In many cases, the opposite may be true.
A young person may postpone marriage because they want to first establish a career.
Another may delay having children because they want to provide better housing or education.
Someone may return to the family home temporarily to save for a house or build financial security.
These decisions can represent greater economic calculation, not less responsibility.
The 2026 UNFPA survey is useful precisely because it challenges the idea that declining or delayed family formation automatically means young people no longer value family life.
India should not turn demographic change into a blame game
India's fertility rate has fallen to around replacement level, and some states are already significantly below it.
That has generated growing discussion about ageing, population growth and the future size of India's workforce.
But demographic change should not be addressed by telling young people when they should marry or how many children they should have.
The more useful question is whether people are able to achieve the family size they themselves want.
UNFPA's approach is important here: the focus should be on reproductive choice and removing barriers rather than creating pressure around population targets.
If a young couple wants children but believes they cannot afford them, that is an economic signal.
If someone wants to marry but cannot find stable employment or affordable housing, that is a labour-market and housing signal.
If a woman wants both a career and a family but expects an unequal caregiving burden, that is a workplace and social-policy signal.
These are problems to solve — not behaviours to shame.
Adulthood should not depend on economic privilege
A wealthy young adult can experiment with careers, rent a home, change jobs and postpone major commitments without immediately facing financial insecurity.
A young person from a lower-income family has much less room for error.
That makes delayed adulthood an inequality issue as much as a generational issue.
India's demographic dividend depends not simply on having millions of young people, but on giving them the economic capacity to build productive and independent lives.
That requires more than degrees.
It requires decent employment, career mobility, affordable housing, accessible healthcare, childcare and social protection.

articles.title: The backstory: From the 'Promised Land' to October 7 - the origin story of Israel-Palestine conflict - The Times of India
articles.summary: The backstory: From the 'Promised Land' to October 7 - the origin story of Israel-Palestine conflict  The Times of IndiaIsrael marks three years since Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks  BBCIsrael’s war on Gaza: Three years in  Frontline Magazine‘Investigate how it happened, don’t let time blur the truth’: Bereaved ex-hostage Sharabi closes Oct. 7 event with plea  The Times of IsraelFear and a far-right lurch: How October 7 reshaped Israel  Al Jaze...
articles.full_text:
Three years ago, Israel experienced one of the deadliest days in its modern history. Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups launched a large-scale attack from Gaza, crossing the border and attacking Israel during a music festival.
More than 1,200 people were killed and 251 people were taken hostage on October 7, 2023, according to the United Nations.
The attack led Israel to launch a massive attack in Gaza that has since reshaped the region but remains unresolved.
So, the question is why conflict resolution is so complicated. The reasons include the history of the two much before October 7, starting with a “promised land”.
In modern political and popular discourse, the Jewish connection to the land is said to be going back 3,000 years. The figure refers to the history of the ancient Israelites and the long-standing Jewish religious connection to the land.
It all begins with Abraham, a biblical patriarch, and the Jewish belief of the “Promised Land”.
Abraham and the 'Promised Land'
Abraham is one of the central figures in the Hebrew Bible and is regarded in Jewish tradition as the first of the three patriarchs of the Jewish people, followed by his son Isaac and grandson Jacob. He is also an important figure in Christianity and Islam.
According to the Book of Genesis, God tells Abraham to leave his homeland and travel to a land that God will show him. That land is subsequently identified in the biblical account as Canaan, an ancient name for a region encompassing parts of present-day Israel and the Palestinian territories, although biblical descriptions of its boundaries vary.
God then promises the land to Abraham's descendants. This becomes the basis of the Jewish concept of the “Promised Land”.
For all the land which thou seest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed for ever.
(Gen. 13:15)
The biblical story continues through Abraham's son Isaac and grandson Jacob, who is given the name Israel. Thus, Jacob's descendants became known as the ‘Children of Israel’.
However, the biblical Land of Israel and the modern State of Israel are not the same thing.
The modern State of Israel was established only in 1948. The biblical story belongs to an ancient religious tradition dating back thousands of years.
For centuries, however, the land remained central to Jewish religious memory. Even after Jews were dispersed across different parts of the world, prayers and religious traditions continued to focus on Jerusalem and the Land of Israel.
"Map of the biblical Land of Canaan and its division among the Twelve Tribes of Israel, as described in the Hebrew Bible (John Bowles, 1760)." (Credit: Library of US Congress, Geography and Map Division)
Ancient homeland to modern political idea
For centuries, the Jewish connection to the Land of Israel remained deeply rooted in religion, history and identity. Even after Jewish communities were dispersed across different parts of the world, Jerusalem and the land remained central to Jewish religious memory and prayer.
By the late 19th century, that ancient connection began to take on a modern political form. Zionism emerged in Europe as a movement seeking Jewish national self-determination and a homeland for Jews, amid growing antisemitism and persecution.
And the territory at the centre of that movement was Palestine, which encompassed much of the land Jews regarded as their historic homeland.
But Palestine was not an empty land waiting for a new population. It was home to a predominantly Arab population, including Muslims and Christians, as well as a longstanding Jewish community.
As Jewish immigration increased, particularly from Europe, two national movements increasingly came to see the same territory as their homeland: the Zionist movement seeking a Jewish national home, and Palestinian Arabs seeking political self-determination in the land where they lived.
That claim to the same territory would become the central question of the conflict that followed.
1917: Britain promises a Jewish national home
The First World War transformed the region.
At the time, Palestine was part of the Ottoman Empire. During the war, Britain fought the Ottoman Empire and eventually took control of the territory.
In 1917, Britain issued the Balfour Declaration, expressing support for the establishment in Palestine of a “national home for the Jewish people”. At the same time, the declaration said that nothing should be done to prejudice the civil and religious rights of the existing non-Jewish communities in Palestine.
For the Zionist movement, the declaration was a major diplomatic breakthrough.
For the Arab population of Palestine, however, the prospect of a Jewish national home in a territory where they were already the majority gave rise to concerns and opposition.
Britain subsequently governed Palestine under a League of Nations mandate. Jewish immigration increased, while relations between Jewish and Arab communities became increasingly tense and violent.
1947: The UN proposes two states
After the Holocaust and the devastation of European Jewry during World War II, international support for a Jewish state grew.
Britain eventually handed the Palestine question to the newly established United Nations.
In 1947, the UN proposed partitioning Palestine into two independent states - one Jewish and one Arab. Jerusalem was to be placed under a special international regime because of its importance to Jews, Muslims and Christians.
Jewish leaders accepted the partition plan but Arab Palestinian leaders and Arab states rejected it.
The dispute soon turned into war.
1948: Israel is born, Palestinians experience the Nakba
On May 14, 1948, David Ben-Gurion, the head of the Jewish Agency and leader of the Jewish community in Palestine, declared the establishment of the State of Israel and became its first prime minister.
The next day, armies from neighbouring Arab states entered the conflict, beginning the first Arab-Israeli war.
Israel not just survived the war but ended up controlling considerably more territory than the Jewish state envisaged under the UN partition plan. The Palestinian Arab state proposed by the UN was never established.
For Palestinians, it meant that more than half of the Palestinian Arab population fled or were expelled., becoming refugees. Palestinians refer to this mass displacement and dispossession as the Nakba, or “catastrophe”.
Thus, many Palestinians and their descendants continue to demand the right to return to homes and properties from which they were displaced, while Palestinian national politics increasingly came to centre on self-determination and statehood.
1967: The land question becomes even more complicated
Another major turning point came nearly two decades later.
During the Six-Day War in 1967, Israel captured the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, along with other territories. The war brought another major displacement of Palestinians and placed the territories at the centre of the conflict that followed.
For Palestinians, the West Bank and Gaza became central to their demand for an independent state, while East Jerusalem became a particularly important part of their national and religious claim. The occupation also meant that about 1.2 million Palestinians came under Israeli military control, as per UN's historical account.
Israel's government and different political and religious groups have had varying positions on the status of the West Bank, with parts of Israeli society viewing the territory through the biblical and historical framework of “Judea and Samaria”, the biblical and historical names for the area now commonly known internationally as the West Bank.
Map showing the modern-day West Bank and surrounding areas,(Credit US Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division)
Israeli settlements were subsequently established in the occupied territories. The settlement issue became one of the most contentious subjects in Israeli-Palestinian negotiations. The UN continues to refer to the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, as occupied Palestinian territory.
This is where the ancient idea of the Promised Land intersects most visibly with the modern conflict.
So where does October 7 fit into this history
By October 7, 2023, the conflict had already passed through major wars in 1948, 1967 and 1973, as well as two Palestinian uprisings known as the Intifadas.
There had also been the Oslo peace process, the split between Hamas and the Palestinian Authority, and repeated rounds of fighting between Israel and Hamas.
At the heart of the unresolved conflict were longstanding disputes over territory, Israeli settlements, Jerusalem, Palestinian refugees, borders and the creation of a Palestinian state.
Then came the Hamas-led attack on Israel three years ago. Israel subsequently launched its war in Gaza.
Three years later, October 7 remains the defining date of the current conflict.
However, as explained, the actual conflict started much before.
Why does the ‘Promised Land’ still matter
The phrase helps explain why the land itself carries such deep meaning.
However, coming back to October 7 and the subsequent conflict, it cannot be explained simply as a religious fight over the land promised to Abraham. The backdrop comes from there but the conflict is the result of several layers of modern history. These include the rise of nationalism, European antisemitism and Jewish immigration, the British Mandate, the Holocaust, the creation of Israel and the displacement of Palestinians.
The “Promised Land” is therefore the beginning of the backstory, not the whole story.
Still, to understand why the conflict has proved so difficult to end, one has to understand something that predates both Israel and Palestine as modern political entities.

articles.title: America already barred birth tourism. So what is US trying to stop now? - The Times of India
articles.summary: America already barred birth tourism. So what is US trying to stop now?  The Times of IndiaBlanche: DOJ working with agencies to tighten visa screening for birth tourism  Baltimore Sun
articles.full_text:
America is more than just a vacation destination for many expectant parents. Some travel to the country with the sole purpose of giving birth on American soil so their child can acquire US citizenship. But this practice has come under scrutiny in the United States, with the Trump administration taking steps to restrict birthright citizenship and curb birth tourism.
In a video posted on Truth Social in May 2023, Trump said that if re-elected as president in the 2024 elections, he would sign an executive order on "day one" to curb birthright citizenship for children of parents who are illegally living in the country.
During his first term, in January 2020, the Trump administration tightened the visa rules for B1 and B2 visas, saying that applications in this category may be rejected if the applicant’s main purpose for travelling to the US is to give birth. If America has already barred birth tourism, what are they trying to stop now?
What is birth tourism?
Birth tourism is the commercial practice in which foreign nationals come to the United States with the primary purpose of giving birth to obtain US citizenship for their child.
On September 23, the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced new visa restrictions targeting foreign nationals who engage in or facilitate commercial birth tourism. It includes:
- Network operators: People who run birth tourism businesses and arrange travel.
- Visa “fixers”: Intermediaries accused of coaching applicants to commit visa fraud, helping them conceal the real purpose of their trip.
- Foreign medical providers: Medical professionals or providers who knowingly facilitate commercial birth tourism.
- Other facilitators: People who knowingly support, assist or enable commercial activity.
The measure is being implemented under Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which allows the State Department to deny visas to foreign nationals whose presence could have serious adverse foreign policy consequences for the US.
Previously, on August 10, the US State Department announced that it had revoked 175,000 visas of foreign nationals who had violated visa terms, including more than 100 visas of North Africans who were alleged to be “birth tourists”.
Who is Rubio targeting.
How does birthright citizenship work?
The 14th Amendment to the US Constitution, passed by Congress in 1866 and ratified in 1868, states that anyone born in the United States is entitled to US citizenship, regardless of their parent’s immigration status.
After returning to the White House, President Donald Trump signed an executive order in January 2025 seeking to restrict citizenship for certain children born in the country to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present in the US.
However, on June 30 this year, the Supreme Court rejected the administration’s attempt to restrict citizenship, ruling that the 14th Amendment guarantees US citizenship to children born in the United States to lawful temporary visitors and undocumented immigrants.
According to the Center for Immigration Studies (CIS), around 20,000 to 25,000 mothers came to the US for birth tourism during 12 months spanning 2016 and 2017. In a separate 2019 analysis, CIS estimated that about 33,000 babies are born annually to women on tourist visas, alongside another 39,000 births to foreign students, guest workers and others on long-term temporary visas, bringing the estimated total to roughly 72,000 births a year to non-immigrants. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recorded a provisional 3.6 million births in the US in 2025.
Birth tourism numbers.
Why is the US seeking to curb birth tourism?
Rubio accused “fixers” of coaching applicants to lie about the real purpose of their travel and charging hefty fees to arrange births in America.
“Foreign commercial networks specialising in birth tourism have exploited the US immigration system to sell US citizenship for profit,” he said.
“By restricting visa issuance of those who both engage in and profit from this fraud, we are sending a clear message: The United States will not allow foreigners to exploit our immigration system and violate the sanctity of US citizenship,” he added.
Dr. Ashok Sharma, Visiting Fellow, University of New South Wales Canberra at Australian Defence Force Academy, told TOI:
How will this policy impact Indians?
The new restriction is likely to impact many Indians seeking temporary visits to the US.
“The policy could lead to stricter scrutiny of applications where consular officers suspect birth-tourism intentions. However, it should not mean automatic denial for genuine visitors. The key issue will be whether applicants can demonstrate a legitimate temporary purpose and their intention to comply with US visa conditions,” said Sharma.
The number of visitor visas issued has risen sharply from pre-COVID levels, increasing from 9.2 million in FY 2019 to 11.7 million in FY 2025.
A new report released last week by the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that Indians seeking visitor visas had to wait 346 days for an interview in FY 2025. According to US State Department data reviewed by the GAO, India accounted for 1,455,255 non-immigrant visa (NIV) applications in the same year.
What prompted the move?
The September 23 measure follows efforts to curb the misuse of birthright citizenship through birth tourism.
A case that previously drew attention involved Chinese billionaire Xu Bo, who reportedly fathered more than 100 children in the US through surrogacy. A surrogate hired for the same, who identified herself as “Judy” to protect her privacy, said she saw an advertisement on Instagram offering $120,000 for surrogacy and was told the intended father was a single man seeking a large family, according to Canadian media outlet CBC News.
Xu also allegedly told a judge during a hearing that he wanted to have 20 or more US-born children, particularly sons, whom he hoped would eventually take over his business. His former partner has alleged he has 300 children, while he has custody of only 12 children born in the US through surrogacy, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Birth tourism fraud case.
What happens next
The constitutional principle of birthright citizenship remains unchanged in the US. The latest policy instead targets those who help make birth tourism possible, from visa “fixers” and medical providers to businesses arranging such trips. The focus is shifting from the child born in the US to the business built around getting there.
For Indians, the policy could bring greater scrutiny at the visa window, with B1/B2 applicants facing closer checks and even longer waits.

articles.title: RBI Repo Rate Hike: Rate Rises to 5.50% - What It Means for Home Loan EMI and FD Rates - The United Indian
articles.summary: RBI Repo Rate Hike: Rate Rises to 5.50% - What It Means for Home Loan EMI and FD Rates  The United Indian
articles.full_text:
The Reserve Bank of India has raised its benchmark policy rate by 25 basis points to 5.50%, marking India's first increase in borrowing costs since February 2023 as inflation risks intensify despite strong economic growth. The decision was announced by Governor Sanjay Malhotra on October 7 after the three-day meeting of the RBI Monetary Policy Committee. All six members supported the increase from 5.25% to 5.50%, while the central bank also shifted its policy stance from “neutral” to “calibrated tightening”.
The repo rate hike could gradually make floating-rate home, auto and personal loans more expensive if banks pass the higher funding cost to borrowers. At the same time, deposit rates could eventually become more attractive if lenders raise interest rates on fixed deposits and other savings products.
So, why did RBI increase repo rate after holding rates steady through several reviews? The central bank said the inflation environment is no longer as benign as it was last year. Consumer inflation rose to about 4.8% in August, while core inflation also increased, signalling that price pressures may be spreading beyond volatile food and fuel categories.
The inflationary pressure has been reinforced by elevated crude oil and commodity prices, the continuing conflict in West Asia, a deficient southwest monsoon and El Niño conditions. RBI said these factors could continue affecting food, fuel and production costs over the coming quarters.
At the same time, India's economy has remained strong enough to give policymakers space to tighten monetary conditions. Real GDP expanded 7.8% in the April-June quarter, stronger than expected, while private consumption, investment and exports continued to support growth. That combination - stronger inflation risks alongside resilient economic activity - ultimately pushed policymakers towards higher rates.
The October RBI Monetary Policy produced changes not only to the repo rate but also to the broader interest-rate corridor and the central bank's policy stance.
| Policy measure | October 2026 decision | 
|---|---|
| Repo rate | 5.50% | 
| Change | +25 basis points | 
| Standing Deposit Facility | 5.25% | 
| MSF rate | 5.75% | 
| Bank Rate | 5.75% | 
| Policy stance | Calibrated tightening | 
| FY27 GDP forecast | 7.1% | 
| FY27 CPI inflation forecast | 5.2% | 
The RBI Monetary Policy Committee unanimously supported the rate increase. However, only four members supported changing the stance to calibrated tightening, while Nagesh Kumar and Ram Singh wanted the stance to remain neutral.
This distinction matters because a policy stance indicates how the central bank views the likely direction of future action.
“Calibrated tightening” does not automatically mean another hike at the next meeting. The RBI's resolution says the stance effectively means rate cuts are off the table in the near term. Future action can involve either another increase or a pause, depending on inflation, growth and how widely price pressures spread. Governor Malhotra later described it as a milder, more data-dependent form of tightening rather than a predetermined series of aggressive increases.
That means discussions around future RBI interest rates will now focus heavily on upcoming inflation data, crude oil prices, food prices and global central-bank decisions. Economists quoted by Reuters expect further increases to remain possible, but estimates vary considerably. Those forecasts are analyst views rather than RBI commitments.
RBI has revised its inflation projection for the current financial year to 5.2%, up from 5.0%. Quarterly projections show pressure becoming particularly visible later in the year:
Core inflation is projected at 4.4% for FY27.
The central bank also noted that headline inflation could average almost 5.8% over the next three quarters. This is why the current inflationary pressure matters even though CPI remains within RBI's legally mandated 2%-6% tolerance band. The central bank's medium-term target remains 4%, and inflation has stayed above that target for several months.
Another reason policymakers were able to act is the strength of domestic activity. When people ask why did RBI increase repo rate despite concerns that higher borrowing costs could slow demand, the answer lies partly in India's stronger-than-expected growth. RBI lifted its FY27 growth projection from 6.7% to 7.1%. Its current projections are:
The central bank says private consumption, investment, services activity and credit flows remain supportive, although weak monsoon conditions and global uncertainty remain risks.
Strong growth provides the RBI with more room to focus on inflation without immediately risking a sharp economic slowdown.
Possibly, but not every borrower will see an immediate increase. A higher repo rate raises the cost at which banks can borrow short-term funds from the central bank. Banks may subsequently increase lending rates, particularly on loans linked to external benchmarks. For floating-rate home-loan borrowers, lenders can respond in several ways:
Mint reports that borrowers with externally benchmarked floating-rate loans are among those most directly exposed to changes in policy rates, although the timing depends on each lender's reset schedule. The repo rate hike does not mean every loan rate automatically rises by exactly 0.25 percentage points on October 7. Fixed-rate borrowers may see no immediate change, while new loans could become more expensive as lenders revise pricing.
Higher RBI interest rates can create a different effect for savers. If banks need to attract more deposits or face higher funding costs, they may raise interest rates offered on fixed deposits and other savings products. However, deposit-rate transmission is determined by individual banks and liquidity conditions. A policy increase does not guarantee that all banks will raise FD rates immediately or by the full 25 basis points.
The banking system is currently operating with significant surplus liquidity, which could reduce the urgency for some banks to aggressively raise deposit rates. Reuters reports that the central bank has chosen not to raise the cash reserve ratio at this stage and instead intends to use instruments such as bond sales and liquidity operations to manage excess funds.
Before the bi-monthly monetary policy announcement, some market participants had expected the RBI to announce additional liquidity-tightening measures. That did not happen. The central bank left reserve requirements unchanged. Malhotra said increasing reserve ratios would be among the least preferred options for withdrawing liquidity.
Instead, the RBI can use tools such as open-market bond sales, variable-rate reverse repo operations and foreign-exchange transactions. This allows policymakers to manage excess liquidity without imposing an immediate additional reserve burden on banks.
The October move is historically significant because it reverses several years of falling or stable borrowing costs. RBI last raised the repo rate in February 2023, when it increased the benchmark by 25 basis points to 6.50%. Rates remained unchanged for an extended period before cuts began in 2025. According to current reports, four reductions during 2025 lowered the repo rate by a combined 125 basis points, eventually taking it to 5.25%.
The October 2026 increase therefore represents the beginning of a new tightening phase. For the bi-monthly monetary policy cycle, that also changes expectations going into the next MPC meeting, scheduled for December 2-4, 2026. The detailed minutes of the October meeting are due on October 21.
The RBI has deliberately avoided promising a fixed path. Whether rates rise again will depend on how inflation evolves, particularly food, energy and core prices. Officials will also monitor whether supply-driven increases become embedded in consumer expectations and company pricing decisions. That is important because monetary policy has limited ability to directly lower international oil prices or improve rainfall, but it can try to prevent temporary shocks from producing persistent inflation.
The third reason why did RBI increase repo rate now is therefore preventive: policymakers are attempting to stop temporary supply shocks from becoming broader and longer-lasting price increases. The RBI Monetary Policy Committee has made clear that further decisions will depend on actual data rather than a predetermined schedule.
For households, the immediate implication is that the era of steadily falling borrowing costs has paused. New and floating-rate loans may become costlier, while savers could eventually see improved deposit returns.
For the economy, the central challenge is now balancing two objectives: preserving India's strong growth momentum while ensuring that the current inflationary pressure does not become entrenched. The October RBI Monetary Policy shows which risk the central bank considers more urgent for now: inflation has risen enough to justify India's first rate increase in nearly four years.

articles.title: India-GCC Cooperation in AI: Innovation & Talent | GHT Ep.8 - Centre for Public Policy Research (CPPR)

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming a strategic driver of economic growth, technological innovation, public-service delivery and national competitiveness. For India and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, AI offers an opportunity to expand a relationship traditionally centred on energy, trade, investment and the Indian diaspora towards a broader partnership based on technology, knowledge and innovation. India brings significant strengths in software development, digital public infrastructure, a large technology talent pool, research capabilities and a growing startup ecosystem. GCC countries, meanwhile, are investing heavily in AI infrastructure, digital transformation, smart cities, education and emerging technologies. These complementary strengths create opportunities for the two sides to move beyond investment towards joint research, talent development, entrepreneurship and the development of AI-enabled solutions.
AI research and innovation can become an important pillar of this emerging partnership. Universities, research institutions, technology companies and innovation centres could collaborate in areas such as generative AI, robotics, semiconductors, cloud computing, cybersecurity, climate resilience, energy efficiency and public-service delivery. Talent and education will also play an equally significant role. Student, faculty and researcher exchanges, joint academic programmes, fellowships, training initiatives and collaborative laboratories could connect India’s large technical talent pool with GCC institutions, research infrastructure and investment opportunities.
AI also presents opportunities in healthcare, education and smart infrastructure. Cooperation could explore AI-assisted healthcare, telemedicine, personalised learning, intelligent transportation, urban planning, energy management, environmental monitoring and digital governance. These applications could provide practical avenues for demonstrating how AI can improve the efficiency and accessibility of public services. The growing AI start-up ecosystem provides another opportunity for deeper economic engagement. Indian start-ups could gain access to GCC markets and capital, while GCC technology ecosystems could benefit from India’s technical expertise and entrepreneurial networks. Start-up exchanges, joint accelerators, venture investment and innovation challenges could facilitate these connections.
At the same time, technological cooperation must be accompanied by responsible AI. India and the GCC can explore dialogue and cooperation on AI governance, data protection, privacy, cybersecurity, transparency and accountability, particularly as AI becomes increasingly integrated into critical sectors. Finally, capacity building will be essential to ensure that AI cooperation produces sustainable outcomes. Combining GCC investment and infrastructure with India’s technical expertise could support workforce reskilling, public-sector training, research capabilities, entrepreneurship and knowledge transfer.
Bharath Reddy is an Associate Fellow with the High-Tech Geopolitics Programme at the Takshashila Institution. His research sits at the intersection of technology, geopolitics, and India’s national interests — focusing on AI governance, open-source technology, and telecommunications. Before turning to policy, he spent 12 years as a telecommunications engineer developing software for 4G base stations. His work aims to bridge the gap between policy and practice in areas such as AI supply chains, Open RAN, and digital infrastructure. His recent work has examined the geopolitics of the AI supply chain, US-China AI competition, generative AI and copyright, and India’s pathway to AI diffusion.
His writing appears in The Hindu, Indian Express, Deccan Herald, ASPI Strategist (Australia), Economic & Political Weekly, and CASI at the University of Pennsylvania. He also manages and co-teaches Takshashila’s Graduate Certificate in Public Policy (Technology and Policy specialisation) and its Politics and Policy of AI course.
Gazi Hassan is a Research Scholar of International Politics. He has an MPhil in International Studies from MMAJ Academy of International Studies in Jamia Millia Islamia University, New Delhi. Was previously associated as a Senior Research Associate with CPPR- Centre for Strategic Studies. Mr. Hassan’s research focuses on the Indo-Pacific, particularly exploring geopolitical dynamics, developments related to trade, terrorism, the role of various actors and including the security dynamics of the region. articles.title: Why India could become a global hub for responsible digital assets innovation - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Why India could become a global hub for responsible digital assets innovation  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Governments and businesses around the world are exploring how blockchain and AI can improve financial systems and digital interactions. From payments and capital markets to identity verification and cross-border transactions, blockchain is increasingly viewed as an important component of the future digital economy.
At the same time, AI is moving beyond generating information to taking actions on behalf of users. As this happens, AI agents will increasingly need ways to interact with financial infrastructure, make payments and execute transactions. For India, recognising the growing convergence between AI and onchain technologies presents an opportunity to shape the next phase of its digital economy. Emerging use cases such as agentic commerce, stablecoin payments and payment standards such as x402 are opening up new possibilities for digital interactions and financial infrastructure.
The question is no longer whether these technologies will become part of the global economy, but which countries will take a leadership role in their development and adoption.
India has the capabilities to become one of these leaders.
A growing talent pool
Alongside a largely tech-savvy population, India has a large pool of talented software developers, engineers and technology professionals. Over the past few decades, this has helped propel India as a key centre for IT services, with the focus now shifting towards entrepreneurship and building product-based companies.
As AI agents become more capable of acting on behalf of users, they will require infrastructure that enables them to securely interact with financial systems, digital assets and payment networks. India's combination of AI talent, blockchain expertise and digital infrastructure gives it a strong foundation to participate in and help shape this transition.
Moreover, over the past decade, India, on the back of Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) and UPI, has built strong digital infrastructure, demonstrating its ability to build and operate complex digital systems at scale.
Innovation beyond digital assets
To grasp the full potential of India, it is important to look beyond digital assets as a concept and explore the potential of blockchain technology more broadly.
Blockchain technology can facilitate innovations through transparency, reduced inefficiencies, security and increased access across areas including cross-border transactions, financial services, supply chains, ecommerce and asset tokenisation.
The convergence of AI and onchain infrastructure could further expand these possibilities. AI can provide the intelligence and automation required to execute increasingly complex tasks, while onchain infrastructure can provide programmable rails through which those actions can be authenticated and settled.
This could enable new forms of agentic commerce, where AI systems interact with businesses, make payments and execute transactions with limited human intervention. Stablecoins and emerging payment standards such as x402 also illustrate how payment infrastructure could evolve for increasingly digital and machine-driven interactions.
The opportunity, therefore, is not simply to add AI to existing products, but to understand how AI and onchain infrastructure can work together to support the next generation of digital commerce.
India is no longer a passive recipient of innovations coming from around the globe. The country is developing its own solutions and increasingly becoming a centre for technology research, product development and innovation.
Why responsible innovation matters
Innovation alone, however, is not enough.
The next phase of digital asset growth will be defined not only by technology, but also by trust, transparency and consumer protection. This becomes particularly important as AI systems become capable of interacting with financial infrastructure and executing transactions on behalf of users.
Policymakers and regulators therefore have an important role to play in creating frameworks that provide clarity, foster innovation and mitigate risks.
Regulatory clarity is increasingly shaping the global environment for digital asset innovation. Europe’s MiCA framework, the US GENIUS Act and the evolving US regulatory framework around market structure and digital assets, including recent actions by the SEC and CFTC, reflect a broader move towards clearer rules for the sector. Australia is also advancing its digital asset framework, with ASIC responsible for licensing and supervising digital asset platforms under the new regime.
For India, this presents an opportunity to develop an approach to digital assets and blockchain that balances innovation with consumer protection and market integrity.
Looking forward
India has an opportunity to become a leader in blockchain and digital asset innovation, supported by the talent to build world-class infrastructure, a strong digital foundation and an entrepreneurial ecosystem capable of driving innovation.
As AI and onchain technologies increasingly converge, India can look beyond the current wave of AI adoption and consider the infrastructure required for a more autonomous digital economy. The growth of agentic commerce, stablecoin payments and programmable financial infrastructure suggests that the next phase of digital transformation will be shaped not by AI or onchain technology in isolation, but by how effectively they work together.
The future of the digital economy is being created today. By combining innovation, talent, infrastructure and thoughtful policy, India can play a meaningful role in shaping this future rather than merely becoming a part of it.

articles.title: RBI MPC hikes repo rate by 25 bps to 5.50%, first increase since February 2023 - cfo.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.summary: RBI MPC hikes repo rate by 25 bps to 5.50%, first increase since February 2023  cfo.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.full_text:
The Reserve Bank of India’s Monetary Policy Committee, chaired by Governor Sanjay Malhotra, on Wednesday raised the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent, marking the first increase in the benchmark rate since February 2023.
The six member MPC held its October meeting from October 5 to 7. The MPC voted unanimously to increase the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent after a detailed assessment of evolving macroeconomic and financial conditions, developments and the outlook, Malhotra announced.
The Standing Deposit Facility rate stands at 5.25 per cent, while the Marginal Standing Facility rate and the Bank Rate stand at 5.75 per cent.
The latest rate hike comes after the RBI’s previous repo rate increase in February 2023, when the central bank raised the policy rate by 25 basis points to 6.50 per cent.
GDP growth projected at 7.1 per cent for FY27
Real GDP growth for FY27 is projected at 7.1 per cent. Growth is projected at 7.2 per cent in Q2 FY27, 6.9 per cent in Q3 FY27 and 6.8 per cent in Q4 FY27.
CPI inflation projected at 5.2 per cent for FY27
CPI inflation for FY27 is projected at 5.2 per cent, with quarterly projections of 4.9 per cent in Q2 FY27, 6 per cent in Q3 FY27 and 5.7 per cent in Q4 FY27.
Core inflation for FY27 is projected at around 4.4 per cent.
Global context remains challenging
“The MPC noted that the global context, on account of geopolitical developments, remains challenging. Nonetheless, the Indian economy has been strong, and the economic momentum remains broad based. Moreover, the economy is expected to remain resilient,” Malhotra said.
The MPC observed that inflation is not as benign as it was last year. Headline CPI inflation is expected to average almost 5.8 per cent in the next three quarters, while core inflation is projected at 4.94 per cent for the financial year, Malhotra said.
Rate cuts off the table
Malhotra said the MPC underscored that, given the current conditions, rate cuts are off the table in the near term. Policy action ahead can only be a rate hike or a pause, depending on evolving conditions and the outlook.
“The duration and extent of the rate hike cycle, therefore, would be contingent on the actual growth inflation development and outlook, especially that of underlying inflation, extent of broadening of price pressure, and speed round effects on the supply shock,” Malhotra said.
Private consumption remains resilient
“Private consumption remained broadly resilient, with continued support from discretionary spending, fixed investment remains strong, as evident from several related indicators,” Malhotra said.
“Some weakness is, however, observed in segments such as non durable goods and domestic air passenger traffic,” he said.
Manufacturing and services activity
Malhotra said manufacturing activity, despite cost pressures, is holding well.
“Service sector activity remained steady and broad based, owing to buoyant domestic and external demand. Both manufacturing PMI and services PMI remained in expansionary zone in Q2,” he said.
Current account deficit remains modest
India’s current account deficit remained modest and well below sustainable levels in Q1 FY27, despite trends in the external sector, Malhotra said.
“The system level financial parameters, as reported even in the last policy statement relating to capital adequacy, liquidity, asset quality, and profitability of the scheduled commercial banks continue to remain robust. Similarly, the system level parameters of NBFCs are also sound,” Malhotra said.
“Notwithstanding robust services trade surplus and net remittance receipts, CAD widened in July due to the higher merchandise trade deficit,” he said.
Merchandise trade deficit widens
India’s merchandise trade deficit increased to $58.7 billion in July and August from $55.1 billion in the same two months last year.
“This is mainly driven by imports of electronic goods and crude oil. Going forward, moderation in global trade growth, elevated energy prices, and persistent trade policy uncertainties pose upside risks to India's current account deficit this year,” Malhotra said.
Forex reserves remain adequate
Malhotra said India’s forex reserves remain adequate.
He also said the RBI remains committed to ensuring orderly adjustments in the exchange rate that are in sync with the underlying macroeconomic fundamentals of the country while curbing excessive volatility.
RBI to set up technical consultative committee for financial markets
In response to rapidly evolving financial market developments, the RBI is planning to constitute a technical consultative committee for financial markets.
The committee will serve as a forum for structured engagement with market participants and other stakeholders on policy and operational matters related to financial markets.
RBI allows interoperability among NBFC account aggregators
The RBI is allowing interoperability among NBFC account aggregators, Malhotra announced.
“We remain committed to ensuring orderly adjustments to the exchange rate that are in sync with the underlying macroeconomic fundamentals of the country and at the same time curbing excessive volatility. First, we are allowing the interoperability. There are a number of account aggregators, as you are aware. We are now allowing the interoperability amongst these NBFC account aggregators,” Malhotra announced.
The RBI is also facilitating SEBI regulated depositories to include information related to deposit accounts in their consolidated account statement, he added.

articles.title: The next order: Will it go to Bangladesh? - Fibre2Fashion
articles.summary: The next order: Will it go to Bangladesh?  Fibre2Fashion
articles.full_text:
Recent media reports suggest some major international fashion retailers are overhauling their global sourcing networks to spread operational, geopolitical and energy risks, with some long-time buyers reportedly shifting work orders from Bangladesh.
According to reports, the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) president has also acknowledged the shift, adding that buyers were increasingly spreading sourcing rather than relying on a single country. For Bangladesh, that is more than a routine change: once buyers start factoring country-level risks more heavily into sourcing, cost and product quality are no longer the only variables.
Least developed country (LDC) graduation is one of those risks, it seems. Bangladesh remains scheduled to graduate on November 24, 2026, although the government has sought a three-year deferment and the process is still pending. The uncertainty matters because LDC preferences underpin Bangladesh’s competitiveness in several major export markets, and graduation does not produce the same outcome in each one.
Buyers therefore have to assess not just when Bangladesh graduates, but what tariff treatment follows in the markets where they source from the country.
The European Union (EU) is of particular importance. Bangladesh will retain Everything But Arms (EBA) preferences for three years after graduation, so there is no immediate loss of duty-free access. Under the current EU arrangement, the benefit runs three years post-graduation. But that gives Bangladesh a window, not a permanent solution.
And the competition inside that window is moving. Vietnam already has an EU free trade agreement (FTA). The EU and India concluded negotiations on their FTA in January, with most tariffs on Indian textiles and apparel set to be removed once it takes effect.
According to estimates, Bangladesh shipped €19.41 billion (~$21.8 billion) of apparel to the EU in 2025 and accounted for 21.57 per cent of the bloc’s apparel import market. The scale of the business makes the comparison with India and Vietnam difficult to dismiss: European buyers are gaining more preferential sourcing options whilst Bangladesh’s post-EBA position remains unsettled.
Energy has meanwhile added a very immediate concern. The recent gas shortage disrupted industrial production and affected shipment schedules, whilst industry groups reported order cancellations and reductions.
One industry survey reportedly found 55 per cent of surveyed knitwear factories had experienced reduced or cancelled orders, 78 per cent partial production shutdowns and 87 per cent shipment delays during the disruption.
According to some reports, factories also faced higher costs from alternative fuel and transportation.
The situation has reportedly improved considerably since. Petrobangla (the state-owned national oil company of Bangladesh) data showed gas supply rising to around 2,600 mmcfd in late September from about 2,300 mmcfd a month earlier, after liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies recovered.
Reports from industry areas also indicated that production has been picking up since, even as the BGMEA president also acknowledged the gas situation had improved significantly.
The bigger question, even if the immediate pressure is easing, is whether the improvement will hold.
That matters because the energy disruption came at precisely the wrong time. Buyers were already reassessing sourcing strategies, and Bangladesh has now given them another variable to consider. A country competing for orders with Vietnam, India and others cannot afford repeated uncertainty over whether factories can maintain production and shipment schedules.
Meanwhile, the BGMEA chief reportedly said that buyers will not necessarily source all their products from one country and that BGMEA was working to attract new buyers whilst encouraging existing ones to increase sourcing from Bangladesh.
He, however, argued that Bangladesh should seek an FTA with the EU within three to four years rather than rely on Generalised Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP Plus).
The argument is particularly relevant now. Bangladesh will retain EBA preferences in the EU for three years after LDC graduation, which would provide additional time. The priority thus should be to use this window to negotiate a longer-term trade arrangement with the EU, rather than allow uncertainty over post-EBA access to become a factor in buyers’ sourcing decisions.
Industry insiders emphasised that the government also needs to make the recent improvement in gas and electricity supply durable. The two issues—trade preferences and energy reliability—are different, but they arrive at the same place: the buyer deciding where the next order goes.
Bangladesh has the factories, capacity and established buyer base. But India is improving its access to the EU whilst Vietnam already has preferential access, and buyers seem more than keen on spreading the risks.
So, whilst Bangladesh is still debating its post-LDC trade future and recovering from an energy shock, the question now is not whether Bangladesh can attract buyers, but whether it can give them enough reasons not to look elsewhere.
