Hitachi High-Tech Corporation has expanded its technology and customer-support footprint in India with the launch of a new demonstration laboratory in the financial capital.
 
In Mumbai, the lab aimed at targeting growing demand for advanced analytical solutions across biopharmaceuticals, environmental applications, materials, chemicals and industrial sectors.
 
The Advanced-Technology Innovation Center Mumbai for analytical systems, established on October 1, is operated by Hitachi High-Tech India Private Limited, the Indian subsidiary of the Hitachi High-Tech Group. 
 
The facility is designed to help customers tackle research and development as well as quality-control challenges through hands-on demonstrations, customer-sample evaluations, application proposals and technical consultations.
 
The Mumbai Lab adds a second specialised technology hub to Hitachi High-Tech’s India operations.
 
In 2025, the company established the Advanced-Technology Innovation Center India in Bengaluru, focusing on the semiconductor sector. 
 
The Bengaluru site is equipped with advanced electron microscopes, including the Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscope (FE-SEM) SU8600, alongside other devices and digital technologies. It supports sample evaluation, failure analysis and process verification while enabling closer collaboration with customers.
 
The new Mumbai facility complements that semiconductor-focused operation by concentrating on analytical applications in chemicals and industrial sectors.
 
At the Mumbai Lab, Hitachi High-Tech has installed analytical systems including spectrophotometers, liquid chromatographs, thermal analyzers, amino acid analyzers and potentiometric titrators.
 
The company plans to use the facility not simply as a product demonstration centre, but as a platform for developing solutions to specific customer problems. Multiple analytical systems can be combined to address complex business requirements, while customer samples can be evaluated on-site to support proof-of-concept work and application development before equipment is deployed.
 
The two-site model gives Hitachi High-Tech a presence across two of India’s rapidly expanding technology and industrial segments: semiconductors through Bengaluru, and chemicals and industrial applications through Mumbai.
 
The company said the approach will expand customer touchpoints and create more opportunities for joint solution development.
 
Hitachi High-Tech also plans to strengthen the provision of digitalised assets supporting HMAX Industry, Hitachi Group’s next-generation solution, with the aim of helping customers address operational challenges and accelerating industrial transformation through the use of physical AI.
 
The Mumbai Lab is located in the Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation (MIDC) area of Thane, around a 60-minute drive from Mumbai Airport.
 
The location provides customers with access to a full-fledged chemical analysis environment designed to meet Indian safety and environmental standards for analytical evaluation of chemical substances.
 
This enables customers to conduct testing and verification using actual samples at the facility, while working directly with Hitachi High-Tech specialists.
 
The company expects the facility to serve a broad range of customers, particularly in biopharmaceuticals, environmental applications, materials, chemicals and other industrial fields.
 
Hitachi High-Tech said it plans to further strengthen its India presence through the two-site laboratory model, while enabling the facilities to independently deliver value to customers in their respective fields.
 
Beyond customer collaboration, the company plans to organise hands-on workshops, work with academic institutions and offer student internships. These initiatives are intended to support scientific and technological development in India while helping build the next generation of technical talent.
 
With the Mumbai and Bengaluru facilities operating as complementary hubs, Hitachi High-Tech is positioning its India operations to provide more localised access to advanced analytical and inspection technologies.
 
The company said it will continue to identify customer challenges and support the advancement of R&D, quality control and industrial capabilities in India through advanced analytical technologies and application-focused solutions.

articles.title: German Mittelstand GCCs in India grow 108% as innovation mandates expand - People Matters - HR News
articles.summary: German Mittelstand GCCs in India grow 108% as innovation mandates expand  People Matters - HR News
articles.full_text:
A new IGCC-ISG report highlights how German mid-sized enterprises are increasingly turning to India for engineering, AI, R&D and product innovation capabilities.
German Mittelstand companies are rapidly expanding their global capability centre (GCC) presence in India, signalling a shift from cost-driven outsourcing to capability-led growth. According to a new report by the Indo-German Chamber of Commerce (IGCC) and Information Services Group (ISG), the number of GCCs established by German mid-sized enterprises in India has increased by 108% over the past five years.
The report points to a broader transformation in the role India plays within German business strategies. Rather than viewing India primarily as a destination for operational efficiencies, German companies are increasingly using the country to drive engineering, artificial intelligence, software development, digital transformation, research and development, and product innovation initiatives.
Today, more than 80 German companies operate over 150 GCC units across India, employing more than 130,000 professionals, according to the report.
Engineering and innovation take centre stage
The latest findings suggest German enterprises are assigning increasingly strategic responsibilities to their India-based centres.
According to the IGCC-ISG report, GCCs established by German Mittelstand companies are moving beyond traditional support services and taking on engineering, technology and innovation-focused mandates. The trend reflects growing demand for software-led products, connected technologies, AI capabilities and digital transformation expertise across German industries.
The report notes that companies are using Indian GCCs to access specialised talent while maintaining control over intellectual property, product ownership and core technical expertise.
Key findings from the report include:
- 108% growth in German Mittelstand GCCs in India over five years.
- More than 80 German firms currently operate over 150 GCC units in the country.
- These centres collectively employ over 130,000 professionals.
- Engineering, AI, software development, R&D and product innovation are becoming core focus areas.
- India's broader GCC ecosystem includes more than 1,700 centres employing over 1.9 million people.
Talent availability drives expansion
The report identifies talent availability as a major factor behind the expansion.
As software, data and AI become increasingly critical to industrial competitiveness, German companies are facing shortages of engineering and digital talent in their home market. India offers access to a large and highly skilled workforce capable of supporting complex technology and innovation programmes.
According to the report, India produces approximately 2.3 million to 2.5 million STEM graduates annually, creating a substantial pipeline of engineering and technology professionals.
The country's established technology hubs, including Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai and the National Capital Region, continue to attract multinational investment due to their mature talent ecosystems and industry networks.
A shift towards capability-led globalisation
The report describes the current trend as a move from an export-oriented operating model towards what it terms "capability-led globalisation".

A Ukrainian drone attack set fire to a Liberian-flagged oil tanker carrying 23 Indian crew members off Russia’s Black Sea coast on Tuesday, with all those aboard later rescued, Russian authorities said.
Russia’s transport ministry said the tanker, Aframax Rio, was attacked by “naval drones” on Tuesday, triggering a fire in the Black Sea near the Russian resort city of Sochi.
The ministry said there were no injuries among the crew, according to Reuters.
The ministry said emergency crews rescued all 23 people aboard the tanker.
The attack caused crude oil to burn openly in the Black Sea, according to the Russian transport ministry.
Firefighters were initially unable to tackle the blaze because of its intensity, but the ministry said they had sufficient means to fight the fire once it became less intense.
Indian crew rescued as tanker catches fire
The vessel was carrying a crew made up entirely of Indian nationals.
The tanker was reported to be on fire off Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, with a large cloud of black smoke visible from Sochi. Authorities in the Sirius federal territory closed beaches following the incident, while water and air quality were being monitored.
“According to atmospheric air quality monitoring data, pollutant concentrations in the Sirius Federal Territory remain many times lower than the maximum permissible concentrations and pose no threat to health,” Dmitry Plishkin, head of the Sirius federal territory administration, said.
The Russian transport ministry said the tanker was attacked by an unmanned vessel.
Attack comes amid wider Black Sea shipping risks
The incident took place amid a series of attacks involving commercial shipping in the Black Sea since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Both Russia and Ukraine have heavily targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea during the conflict. Russia has in recent days attacked grain vessels carrying Ukrainian goods near the coast of Romania.
Earlier on Tuesday, a Russian strike on a merchant vessel flying the Marshall Islands flag in the Black Sea killed at least one crew member and injured several others.
The vessel was carrying rapeseed oil and caught fire after its superstructure was damaged.
Two other merchant ships, the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and Palau-flagged Able, were also hit by drones of unknown origin about 112 kilometres off Bulgaria’s coast.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denied that Ukrainian forces were behind those strikes near Bulgaria.
Sochi coast placed under restrictions
Videos and photographs circulated on social media showed large flames burning offshore and a thick column of black smoke over Sochi.
Sochi Mayor said access to the coast and beaches was being restricted. Beaches in Sirius were also closed following the tanker fire.
The Aframax Rio was reportedly near the Russian coast when the attack took place. Russian independent media had reported the incident, while MarineTraffic had last located the tanker in the Black Sea near the Russia-Georgia border.
The vessel was included on Ukraine’s sanctions list as part of Russia’s so-called “shadow fleet”, according to The Kyiv Independent.
India raises concern over attacks on shipping
The tanker incident comes amid attacks on commercial vessels in other key maritime routes involving Indian crew members.
The ministry of external affairs had earlier condemned an attack on MV Royad Mammadov in the Black Sea, in which two foreign seafarers were killed and some crew members, including three Indian nationals, were injured. The three Indians were reported safe after receiving medical treatment in Romania.
The MEA also condemned an attack on the Panama-flagged MT On Peace off Oman while it was transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The vessel had 19 crew members, including 17 Indians, and 12 crew members were injured, including 11 Indians, according to the ministry.
The MEA said India viewed attacks on commercial shipping and seafarers with “grave concern” and called for dialogue and diplomacy to end ongoing conflicts.
In September, India and Liberia also launched a 25-nation “Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers” at the UN General Assembly to work towards the safety and security of merchant crews and commercial shipping against targeted attacks, according to the MEA.

articles.title: India better off risking US market access than abandoning Russian oil: Political Economist - Big News Network.com
articles.summary: India better off risking US market access than abandoning Russian oil: Political Economist  Big News Network.com
articles.full_text:
London [UK], October 6 (ANI): India would be better off accepting the risk of losing some access to the US market than abandoning Russian oil purchases if forced to choose between the two, political economist Gautam Sen said, arguing that a disruption to energy supplies could impose a much higher cost on the Indian economy.
The assessment highlights the difficult trade-off facing India as energy security becomes increasingly entangled with trade and geopolitics, even as the United States remains India's largest merchandise export market and New Delhi depends on imports for nearly nine-tenths of its crude oil requirement.
"It is better to accept the punishment of loss of markets. It's a question of two evils," Sen, a former London School of Economics faculty member, told ANI in an interview.
Sen argued that further trade concessions may not be sufficient to resolve differences with Washington if India's relationship with Russia, particularly its oil purchases, remains part of the wider geopolitical friction.
"US will be very difficult to satisfy with any further trade concessions India might attempt to make. And India has already made significant concessions to the US," he said.
He said stopping purchases of Russian crude could push up India's energy costs by forcing refiners to look for alternative supplies in an already tight global market.
"If India stops purchasing Russian oil, it will be extremely consequential for India because the prices will rise in the global market," Sen said.
The stakes are significant on both sides of that equation.
The United States is India's largest merchandise export destination, accounting for about 20.75 per cent of India's exports, according to the Department of Commerce's Trade Intelligence and Analytics portal. The portal puts India's merchandise exports to the US at over USD 92 billion, underlining the importance of continued access to the American market.
At the same time, India's exposure to movements in global oil markets remains substantial. Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell data showed the country's crude oil import dependence at around 88 per cent, meaning a sharp increase in international crude prices can feed through to India's import bill, inflation, the rupee and broader macroeconomic conditions.
That makes access to competitively priced crude an important economic consideration for New Delhi even as it seeks deeper commercial ties with Washington.
India and the US had in February announced a framework for an interim trade agreement under which India agreed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on a range of US industrial and agricultural goods, while the United States said it would apply an 18 per cent reciprocal tariff on originating Indian goods, with relief envisaged for certain products subject to successful conclusion of the agreement.
Negotiations continued subsequently. During US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer's visit to New Delhi in June, the two sides said they had made "substantial progress" and were working towards an interim agreement covering market access, non-tariff barriers, digital trade and supply-chain resilience.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump also reviewed cooperation in trade, energy and other areas during a telephone conversation on September 30, with both sides agreeing to remain engaged.
Sen, however, said he believed the negotiations had currently reached an impasse after substantial efforts by the Indian side.
"It is now deadlocked. But deadlocked does not mean forever," he said. "It is deadlocked at the moment."
His assessment suggests that the larger question for India may no longer be simply how many trade concessions it can offer, but how far it can deepen economic ties with the US without compromising an energy strategy shaped by its heavy dependence on imported crude. (ANI)

articles.title: India’s ‘million mutinies’ are puncturing Modi’s aura of invincibility - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: India’s ‘million mutinies’ are puncturing Modi’s aura of invincibility  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
This October, India is a country where a million mutinies are gathering force.
India’s “cockroaches” — supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) — are back on the streets, marking Mahatma Gandhi’s 157th birth anniversary with non-violent disobedience. Once again, the atmosphere was carnival-like: plenty of students; a phalanx of marching, fist-waving women, arm-in-arm with young men, punching the air and shouting: “Gyanu, it’s done, bro”.
Recommended Stories
Surreally enough, they already talk of “Gyanu” — India’s Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar — in the past tense. What will follow — what system or person — is a question that has been put on hold. That’s for later. For now, the protestors are unified with a single, concentrated message: they want Kumar, accused of manipulating voter rolls in favour of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party, to resign.
Young women and queer students have taken to the streets over women’s safety in Delhi after a 17-year-old girl was allegedly gang-raped in Aastha Kunj Park in southeast Delhi by three men who posed as police officers. Concurrently in Mumbai, the parents of Sahil Wakode, a second-year BTech student at IIT Bombay, have launched an indefinite hunger strike after he died by suicide earlier this month. They are demanding the arrest of his teachers and alleging severe caste-based harassment. In Pune, Maharashtra Public Service Commission aspirants are on the streets demanding the chairman’s resignation over a range of concerns about alleged examination irregularities, transparency issues and uncertainty surrounding examination results.
The rest of India — those not out on the streets — is umbilically tethered to a computer or phone screen, riding alternating currents of buoyancy, pessimism, doubt and rage.
The sudden convergence of these volatile protests has effectively caught the Modi government in a pincer movement of domestic unrest. The overlapping waves of unrest represent a dangerous shift in the national mood, effectively uniting a fragmented Gen Z demographic against the Centre, re-energising and bringing together the opposition as a national force, and transforming disparate grievances into a cohesive, highly visible movement that the government can no longer contain.
Besides, central Delhi and parts of Mumbai are locked down under heavy security — on Gandhi Jayanti, no less — compounding the crisis of optics. Modi no longer provides stable governance. At this point, he rules not by legitimacy but by brute force and fear — of losing power and the legal reckoning that might follow once power is lost. For much of Modi’s political history, hierarchy has carried its own justification. His foundational axiom is that voters work for him and not the other way around. When he was popular, it worked. He could get us to queue in front of ATMs; lock us down without food, money, or scientific justification; abrogate Kashmir’s special constitutional status and beat up farmers and students.
When he was no longer popular, with the Election Commissioner — protected by lifelong immunity — tilting the system in his favour, he could dispense with popularity as well as a popular mandate altogether. But he no longer has the luxury of power without consequence. For three terms he wielded the combined power of popular legitimacy and institutional control. That era has ended. He no longer has a mandate like the one he had in 2014, and no institution — media, parliament, election commission or judiciary — is left to absorb the shock on his behalf.
The protests are disparate, but their underlying demand is strikingly similar: power comes with responsibility. The Chief Election Commissioner, the upper-caste teachers at IIT Bombay and the gang rapists who posed as cops are all being pulled into the same reckoning.
After the CJP’s first victory in July — which culminated in the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan — Modi retreated into his office, with some of his old swagger missing. Pierced by the relentless ridicule of Instagram reels and memes, the giant balloon that is Modi’s self-esteem is leaking from a thousand cuts. History will note that the first cracks in his powerful regime appeared not with an electoral defeat but when ordinary students stopped believing that nothing can be done.
This new wave of protests, the second in three months, challenges the inevitability of Modi.
The nationwide protests will continue all through October. Besides the “cockroaches”, India’s opposition parties will organise five big rallies around the nation. Besides the demand for Kumar’s resignation, the parties want a return to ballot papers, rather than Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs), arguing that electronic voting has made the recording and counting of votes vulnerable to manipulation. Leader of the opposition, Rahul Gandhi, has accused Kumar of high treason and warned of consequences once he is removed from the post.
Modi, meanwhile, has no plans to yield any of his authority.
He began the day at Gandhi’s samadhi, laying flowers before the apostle of non-violence while deploying paramilitary cordons and anti-riot vehicles across Delhi and Mumbai to stop protestors from gathering. Roads leading to Jantar Mantar in New Delhi — the designated protest site — are barricaded. The few who get past the blockades are being detained by police. The irony is almost too neat to be accidental. There were mass detentions on Friday. Fresh detentions on Saturday. Despite repeated detentions, protestors keep returning to the sites, pressing their demands.
Modi has, in fact, revived some of the very instruments of repression that Gandhi spent his political life resisting: restrictions on public assembly, curfews, preventive detention and the policing of dissent. The more precarious his hold on power, the more nakedly he reaches for brute force.
If there’s anything Gandhi taught, it was the limits of power and force.
Over the coming days, Modi may well succeed in emptying the streets, imprisoning protesters, confiscating placards and silencing dissent. What he will not be able to do, at least not indefinitely, is compel Indian voters to believe that power is legitimate simply because it is powerful.
In an exhausted democracy like India’s — with its institutions crumbling under the weight of unchecked power — the sight of Indians rising in a million mutinies is one of the more beautiful things I have seen in my life. The month of agitations is going to be messy, irreverent and noisy. The spectacle will also invite romanticism. There will be a temptation, when looking at this young movement with such extraordinary visual energy, to dwell on its purity, youthful exuberance, or incandescent rage.
It would be a mistake.
India’s new protest culture should neither be romanticised nor categorised in some tight box. It is something more, something rare: it is unfinished.

Three civilians have been killed and 36 injured in Houthi-claimed attacks on two airports in Saudi Arabia, according to a statement from the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
The attack on Abha International Airport killed two female residents, a Moroccan and an Algerian, and injured 28 others, GACA reported.
The attack on King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh killed a Sudanese citizen and injured eight residents, including five Saudi citizens.
GACA said it is working “in full integration and continuous coordination with the relevant security authorities” to assess the damage and take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and workers.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, said forces intercepted a ballistic missile north of Riyadh and destroyed a platform in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, that had been used to launch attacks on the Saudi capital.
Previous attacks on Saudi airports
New cage-like fences have been erected this week around fuel tanks and other equipment of the Saudi state-run Aramco oil company near the Riyadh airport.
On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards the airport in Riyadh from Yemen.
A day later, on September 19, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport.
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces from the country’s internationally recognised government are locked in escalating combat with Iran-aligned Houthi forces who seized a broad swathe of territory astride the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government said the Houthis launched ballistic missiles and drones against Aden airport early on Wednesday. No casualties were reported.
Meanwhile, the United States embassy in Riyadh has issued another security alert for Americans in Saudi Arabia due to the ongoing security situation, reminding “all US citizens to exercise heightened vigilance”.

Oman’s air force has evacuated 10 crew members of a Panamanian-flagged oil tanker following an attack in the Strait of Hormuz.
The On Peace tanker was struck 9 nautical miles (about 17km) off the Omani port city of Limah on Tuesday, according to the Omani Ministry of Defence. The attack set off a fire on board the vessel.
“The crew members were transported to the Khasab hospital in Musandam governorate and received medical treatment,” the ministry said in a statement on X.
No group has claimed the attack so far.
It comes as security in the Strait of Hormuz continues to deteriorate amid the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
India’s foreign ministry, the Ministry of External Affairs, said at least 12 of the ship’s 19 crew members were injured when a projectile hit the vessel as it transited the strait. Seventeen of the 19 crew members were Indian nationals, it said, as were 11 of the injured.
“The continuing incidents of attacks on shipping in the region remain a cause of deep concern for India,” the ministry said. “We reiterate our call for an immediate cessation of such attacks in the interests of peace and stability in the region.”
India is one of the largest contributors of sailors to merchant shipping worldwide. The Indian government said in July that at least 10 Indian seafarers had been killed since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February. Another attack on a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz in September also killed an Indian sailor.
Iran effectively closed the waterway after the US-Israel war began on February 28. It has frequently attacked commercial vessels that do not use its designated route in the waterway, and has said it wants to charge ships for passage.
At least seven other incidents involving tankers have been reported in the past week, according to Marisks, a shipping intelligence service.
Despite the attacks, oil exports from the Middle East have risen to pre-war levels in recent weeks.
The seven-day moving average of Middle East crude exports reached 18.3 million barrels per day (bpd) on September 30, compared with about 18 million bpd on average in the 12 months before the war, according to provisional data from Kpler, a data firm.
Still, prices remain high, with Brent crude futures rising to $101.51 a barrel on Tuesday, compared with $72.48 the day before the war began.
